---
engine: markdown
title: "rush run"
---

The `run` command evaluates an R expression and prints (or saves) the result.
It is the core command of `rush`.

## Usage

```bash
rush run [options] [<expression>] [--] [<file>...]
```

## Simple expressions

At its core, `rush run` evaluates any R expression and prints the result:

```{term}
rush run '6 * 7'
```

Multiple semicolon-separated expressions work; the value of the last one is printed:

```{term}
rush run 'x <- 1:10; mean(x)'
```

Strings, vectors, and lists all print naturally:

```{term}
rush run 'paste("Hello", "from", "R", sep = ", ")'
```

```{term}
rush run 'rev(LETTERS[1:8])'
```

## Reading input files

Pass a file path after the expression, and it is read into a data frame called `df`:

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

```{term}
rush run 'nrow(df)' mtcars.csv
```

With just a file and no expression, the data is printed. A quick way to peek:

```{term}
rush run 'head(df, 5)' mtcars.csv
```

### The `df` and `dfs` variables

Two variables are always available in your expression:

- **`df`**: the first input (a data frame for flat files, or a named list of
  tables for database files).
- **`dfs`**: a named list of all inputs, keyed by file stem. Database entries
  are nested one level deeper: `dfs$dbname$tablename`.

```{term}
rush run 'names(dfs)' mtcars.csv
```

### Reading from standard input

Use `-` to read from stdin. This makes `rush` composable in shell pipelines:

```{term}
echo "name,score
Alice,92
Bob,85
Carol,97" | rush run 'df |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(score))' -
```

You can pipe the output of one `rush` into another:

```{term}
rush run 'head(df, 5)' mtcars.csv | rush run 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, cyl, hp)' -
```

Use `-F` to read non-CSV formats from stdin, for example JSON:

```{term}
rush run -O json 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | rush run -F json 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, hp)' -
```

### Reading DuckDB databases

Point `rush` at a `.duckdb` file and all tables are loaded into `dfs`:

```{term}
rush convert -o mtcars.duckdb mtcars.csv
rush run 'names(dfs$mtcars)' mtcars.duckdb
```

## Options

### `--delimiter` (`-d`)

Override the delimiter for both reading and writing:

```{term}
rush run -d "\t" 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | cat
```

### `--no-header` (`-H`)

Suppress headers on both input and output. Input columns are auto-named
`x1`, `x2`, ...:

```{term}
echo -e "10\n20\n30\n40\n50" | rush run -H 'sum(df$x1)' -
```

```{term}
seq 5 | rush run -H 'cumsum(df$x1)' -
```

### `--no-input-header`

Read without a header row, but still include a header in the output:

```{term}
seq 5 | rush run --no-input-header 'cumsum(df$x1)' -
```

### `--no-output-header`

Read normally but omit the header row from the output:

```{term}
rush run --no-output-header 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | cat
```

### `--names`

Provide explicit column names (comma-separated). Implies `--no-input-header`:

```{term}
echo -e "1,Alice\n2,Bob" | rush run --names "id,name" 'df'
```

### `--no-clean-names` (`-C`)

By default, `rush` normalizes column names (lowercase, underscores). Disable
with `-C` to preserve the originals:

```{term}
echo "First Name,Last Name,Score (%)
Alice,Smith,92" | rush run 'names(df)' -
```

```{term}
echo "First Name,Last Name,Score (%)
Alice,Smith,92" | rush run -C 'names(df)' -
```

### `--tidyverse` (`-t`)

Load the entire Tidyverse (plus glue) so you can use dplyr, tidyr, stringr,
etc. without qualifying names:

```{term}
rush run -t 'df |> group_by(cyl) |> summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg)) |> arrange(desc(avg_mpg))' mtcars.csv
```

### `--library` (`-l`)

Load specific packages. Comma-separate multiple packages:

```{term}
rush run -l stringr 'stringr::str_to_title("hello world")'
```

```{term}
rush run -l dplyr,tidyr 'df |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(mpg, hp), names_to = "metric") |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 4)' mtcars.csv
```

### `--seed`

Set the random seed for reproducible results:

```{term}
rush run --seed 42 'sample(1:100, 5)'
```

Run it again; same seed, same result:

```{term}
rush run --seed 42 'sample(1:100, 5)'
```

### `--output` (`-o`)

Write the result to a file instead of stdout. The output format is inferred from
the extension:

```{term}
rush run -o summary.csv 'data.frame(stat = c("min", "mean", "max"),
                                     mpg = c(min(df$mpg), mean(df$mpg), max(df$mpg)))' mtcars.csv
cat summary.csv
```

Write to Parquet:

```{term}
rush run -o subset.parquet 'dplyr::filter(df, mpg > 25)' mtcars.csv
rush run 'df' subset.parquet
```

### `--output-root`, `--output-record`

Customize the XML element names when writing XML. Defaults are `root`
(root) and `record` (each record). Also used by TOML for the record name:

```{term}
rush run -n -O xml --output-root garage --output-record car 'head(df)' mtcars.csv
```

### `--dry-run` (`-n`)

Print the generated script instead of running it. Great for learning what `rush`
does under the hood, or for saving scripts:

```{term}
rush run -n 'df |> dplyr::filter(mpg > 25)' mtcars.csv
```

### `--no-ir` (`-I`)

Run with plain `Rscript` instead of `ir`. No package resolution happens --
everything must already be installed:

```{term}
rush run -I '2 + 2'
```

### `--verbose` (`-v`)

Show parsed arguments before running. Useful for debugging complex invocations:

```{term}
rush run -v --seed 7 'sum(1:10)' 2>&1
```

## Help

```{term}
rush run -h
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv mtcars.duckdb summary.csv subset.parquet
```
